title: 'I cannot believe my boy is gone'
subtitle: Long-delayed coroner's inquest into 2013 fatal police shooting of 18-year-old begins
article: More than a decade after Sammy Yatim was shot dead by a Toronto police officer, his grieving family told a long-delayed coroner's inquest that they remain traumatized, and called for greater supports for relatives of people killed by police.
Yatim's death "paralyzed me, locked me in my grief and depression, destroyed my life," said an emotional Sahar Bahadi, his mom and the first witness called at the inquest. "It shattered my dreams."

Mandatory in Ontario after every death involving police, coroner's inquests probe the circumstances of a death and typically result in recommendations aimed at preventing future fatalities. The estimated 10-day inquest into Yatim's shooting has a limited focus - in part because the circumstances of the 2013 fatal shooting have already been subject to a highly publicized criminal trial, said coroner's counsel Peter Napier in his opening address.

Instead, the inquest will explore how to improve police decision-making, exploring topics including police forces' hiring and screening practices, the role of police bystanders in deadly confrontations, and what supervisors can do when "red flags" arise with problem cops.

"What recourse do police agencies have when an officer does make repeated bad decisions? How do police respond when an officer has a number of use-of-force reports? When an officer draws their firearm too frequently?" Napier said, running the inquest's five jurors through questions they might ask during the proceeding.
The inquest will also examine how to improve police calls involving people in mental health crisis and the availability of mental health support for officers.

Yatim, 18, was shot eight times by then-Const. James Forcillo on July 27, 2013, while alone on a Toronto streetcar. The fatal encounter was captured on video, showing Forcillo repeatedly firing on Yatim even as he lay prone on the ground, prompting national outrage.

Police had been called after Yatim pulled out a knife and exposed himself on a busy Dundas streetcar, stalling the vehicle and sending passengers flooding out the doors. Forcillo fired upon Yatim, who was by then solo on the streetcar, less than a minute after arriving at the scene.

In 2016, a jury convicted Forcillo of attempted murder in Yatim's shooting, an outcome made possible by Crown prosecutors' decision to split the nine shots Forcillo fired into two distinct volleys with separate criminal charges. Forcillo, who resigned from the Toronto police, was sentenced to six years in jail and was granted full parole in 2020.

The former officer is scheduled to testify later in the coroner's inquest, alongside other witness officers, including Const. Iris Fleckeisen, Forcillo's partner on the night of the shooting, police employees tasked with hiring and training, and experts in officer behaviour and wellness.
Overseen by Ontario coroner Dr. David Cameron, the inquest began with comments from Forcillo's family, who said they still experience daily struggles accepting Yatim's death.

"For the past 10 years, I have not been well. I still am not well. I fight every single day just to get out of bed," Sara Yatim, Sammy's younger sister, said in a written statement read out to jurors.
In it, she lamented that her life had been changed in one fateful minute. The shooting "made me lose hope in myself, the world and our society," Sara Yatim said.
"Sammy probably just needed a hug," she wrote.

Alongside her parents, Sara called for greater mental health and financial support for people who have been through similar traumas. Bahadi, Sammy's mother, noted the family had only recently moved to Canada from Syria at the time of Sammy's death, saying they'd struggled financially while trying to recover from his killing.

In his statement, read out by lawyer Ed Upenieks, Sammy's father Bill Yatim said he misses his quiet boy who loved animals, his friends, art and movies featuring Mr. Bean. He recalled that Sammy used the first paycheck from his part-time job working at McDonald's to buy a TTC Metropass.

"I think about him all of the time. I cannot believe my boy is gone. I see someone walking down the street that looks like him and I jump. I am left with a terrible sense of emptiness and loneliness," Bill Yatim wrote.
He called for the inquest to produce recommendations that can help design a better public safety system.
"We cannot let Sammy's blood to have been spilled in vain," he said.

The inquest was initially scheduled to begin in November 2022, but was delayed at the last minute by an 11th-hour motion brought by Forcillo's lawyer seeking to explore the possibility Yatim wanted to die by suicide and provoked a fatal police shooting.
That request was later denied by Cameron, the presiding coroner, who said there was no direct evidence suggesting Yatim wished to end his life through a confrontation with police.
The inquest continues Tuesday.
